main.title: Babbage demonstrates the Difference Engine
main.summary: Charles Babbage demonstrated a partially assembled Difference Engine in 1833. Designed in the 1820s, his mechanical calculator used the method of finite differences to calculate mathematical tables.

cards.heading: Babbage demonstrates the Difference Engine
cards.text:
Charles Babbage demonstrated a partially assembled Difference Engine in 1833. Designed in the 1820s, his mechanical calculator used the method of finite differences to calculate mathematical tables.

A difference engine is an automatic mechanical calculator designed to tabulate polynomial functions. It was designed in the 1820s, and was created by Charles Babbage. The name difference engine is derived from the method of finite differences, a way to interpolate or tabulate functions by using a small set of polynomial co-efficients. Some of the most common mathematical functions used in engineering, science and navigation are built from logarithmic and trigonometric functions, which can be approximated by polynomials, so a difference engine can compute many useful tables.

main.title: Phenakistoscope
main.summary: The phenakistoscope (also known by the spellings phénakisticope or phenakistiscope) was the first widespread animation device that created a fluid illusion of motion.

cards.heading: Phenakistoscope
cards.text: The phenakistoscope (also known by the spellings phénakisticope or phenakistiscope) was the first widespread animation device that created a fluid illusion of motion. Dubbed Fantascope and Stroboscopische Scheiben ('stroboscopic discs') by its inventors, it has been known under many other names until the French product name Phénakisticope became common (along with alternative spellings). The phenakistiscope is regarded as one of the first forms of moving media entertainment that paved the way for the future motion picture and film industry. Similar to a GIF animation, it displays a short continuous loop.

main.title: Analytical engine
main.summary: The analytical engine was a proposed digital mechanical general-purpose computer designed by the English mathematician and computer pioneer Charles Babbage.

cards.heading: Analytical engine
cards.text:
The analytical engine was a proposed digital mechanical general-purpose computer designed by the English mathematician and computer pioneer Charles Babbage. It was first described in 1837 as the successor to Babbage's difference engine, which was a design for a simpler mechanical calculator.

The analytical engine incorporated an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), control flow in the form of conditional branching and loops, and integrated memory, making it the first design for a general-purpose computer that could be described in modern terms as Turing-complete. In other words, the structure of the analytical engine was essentially the same as that which has dominated computer design in the electronic era.

Babbage was never able to complete construction of any of his machines due to conflicts with his chief engineer and inadequate funding. It was not until 1941 that Konrad Zuse built the first general-purpose computer, Z3, more than a century after Babbage had proposed the pioneering analytical engine.

main.title: Morse develops his electrical telegraph
main.summary: Samuel Morse developed a recording electrical telegraph in 1837. Electrical telegraphy sent messages between distant stations through electric signals over wires.

cards.heading: Morse develops his electrical telegraph
cards.text: Samuel Morse developed a recording electrical telegraph in 1837. Messages travelled as electrical signals along wires between distant offices, reaching their destination much faster than a letter carried by hand. Telegraph lines, often suspended from poles, became an important communications network from the 1840s onwards. Different systems turned the signals into readable information in different ways. In needle telegraphs, an electric current moved a pointer towards a letter on a printed list. Early designs needed several needles and separate wires. The practical challenge was to turn an electrical change at one station into an intelligible message at another.

main.title: Daguerreotype
main.summary: Daguerreotype was the first publicly available photographic process, widely used from the 1830s to 1850s.

cards.heading: Daguerreotype
cards.text: Louis Daguerre introduced his photographic process in 1839. A polished sheet of silver-plated copper was treated with fumes to make it sensitive to light, then exposed inside a camera. Mercury vapour revealed the image, and further chemical treatment stopped it reacting to light. The finished surface was delicate, so it was sealed behind glass. Exposure could take seconds in bright sunshine or much longer in dim conditions. The daguerreotype became the first publicly available photographic process, before cheaper methods such as the ambrotype largely replaced it by 1856.

main.title: Penny Black
main.summary: The Penny Black was the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system.

cards.heading: Penny Black
cards.text:
The Penny Black was the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system. It was first issued in the United Kingdom on 1 May 1840 but was not valid for use until 6 May. The stamp features a profile of 21-year-old Queen Victoria.

In 1837, British postal rates were high, complex, and anomalous. To simplify matters, Sir Rowland Hill proposed an adhesive stamp to indicate pre-payment of postage. At the time it was normal for the recipient to pay postage on delivery, charged by the sheet and on distance travelled. By contrast, the Penny Black allowed letters of up to 1⁄2 ounce (14 grams) to be delivered at a flat rate of one penny, regardless of distance.

main.title: Ada Lovelace: the Analytical Engine notes
main.summary: In 1843, Ada Lovelace published her translation of Menabrea’s account of the Analytical Engine, adding extensive notes on its possibilities.

cards.heading: Ada Lovelace: the Analytical Engine notes
cards.text: In 1843, Ada Lovelace published her translation of Menabrea's account of Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, adding extensive notes on its possibilities. She recognised that the machine could have applications beyond calculation, an insight central to her reputation as an early computer programmer. The English mathematician and writer, born Augusta Ada Byron in 1815, studied the proposed mechanical general-purpose computer while its capabilities were still being imagined. Her notes connect a design for machinery to a broader conception of what such a machine could do.

main.title: Morse code enters use
main.summary: American Morse code entered use in 1844, encoding messages as sequences of short and long signals. Its development involved Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail; later revisions produced the international code.

cards.heading: Morse code enters use
cards.text: American Morse code entered use in 1844, turning letters into sequences of short and long signals: dots and dashes. Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail developed the system, with Vail providing an alphabet-based code for commercial telegraphy in North America. Friedrich Gerke later simplified it for European use, helping establish the international version. A message depended on recognisable differences in duration and spacing, allowing its receiver to reconstruct words from a succession of pulses. The international code covers letters, numbers, punctuation and procedural signals, making the same basic method useful across different communications equipment.

main.title: The Knickerbocker baseball rules
main.subtitle: A developing game finds a written framework
main.summary: The New York Knickerbocker club compiled baseball rules in 1845, an important stage in a much older game's development.

cards.heading: A developing game finds a written framework
cards.text: New York's Knickerbocker Base Ball Club compiled an influential set of rules in 1845. They defined fair and foul ground, prohibited putting runners out by throwing the ball at them and specified three outs before changing sides. A notable match using the code took place at Elysian Fields in Hoboken on June 19, 1846. Pitchers delivered underhand, and a contest could run to twenty-one runs. The written framework helped shape the game's continued development towards modern baseball.

main.title: Rugby School writes its football laws
main.subtitle: A school code travels with its players
main.summary: Pupils at Rugby School drew up written football laws in 1845, a documented milestone in rugby's development.

cards.heading: A school code travels with its players
cards.text: Three Rugby School pupils drew up written football laws in 1845. Printed in a pocket-sized book, the code helped define the school's game and included terms such as the try. Former pupils carried those practices to universities and clubs, where written rules made it easier to organise matches. School traditions, this published code and later organisations together shaped rugby's development.
